method: One NTP exchange gives the offset of the server clock relative to the client clock and the round-trip delay, exactly as RFC 5905 section 8 defines them: offset = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2 and delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2), where T1 is when the client sent the request, T2 when the server received it, T3 when the server sent the reply and T4 when the client received it. T1 and T4 come from the client clock and T2 and T3 from the server's, so only the differences inside each pair are used and any fixed origin works on each side. A positive offset means the server clock reads ahead, so adding it to a local reading gives the server's time and the local clock is that far slow. The request and the reply are assumed to take the same time on the wire, which leaves the true offset within half the delay of the estimate: a narrow delay gives a tight answer and a wide one a loose answer. A negative delay is arithmetically possible, as RFC 5905 notes when the two clocks run at different frequencies, but it cannot come from a sound exchange, so the page refuses those figures instead of clamping the delay to a precision floor. Each timestamp accepts 0 to 1,000,000,000,000 seconds with up to 12 decimal places, and the arithmetic is carried in integer picoseconds so epoch-sized readings keep every digit the input holds. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.
